units.spoken: Actor-Critic: A2C and A3C
A second network judges each move a few steps after it is made.
Learning from whole games makes each move wait until the game ends to be judged, and then the judgement is noisy.
Section one, The same Pong paddle

The running example is Atari Pong. The state is the screen, a stack of the last few frames. The moves are up, stay and down; one move is one step. The reward is plus 1 for a point won, minus 1 for a point lost, 0 on every other step. J, the average net points per game, is what learning tries to raise.

Take a look at this figure. The court is the state: the ball's place and the paddle's height are what the networks read. The paddle can only move up, stay, or down, so every choice is one of three moves. The ball coming toward the paddle is the moment a move matters. This one screen, one paddle, one ball is the whole running example for the page.

sections.section: 2 A critic that judges moves early

units.spoken: Section two, A critic that judges moves early
The critic scores the move from one screen

Picture the paddle sliding up to return the ball, long before the point ends. A second network, the critic, reads the screen right after the move and guesses the value of that screen, the return still to come from it, so the move is scored at once instead of waiting for the game to end.
How. The critic learns from each step: it compares its guess with what actually followed, the reward plus its guess for the next screen, and moves its guess toward that target.
When it works, moves are judged a few steps after they are made, so learning no longer waits for whole games to end.

It is the value network, V of s with weights fee, of REINFORCE. The actor is the policy network that picks the moves, the same network REINFORCE trained. Methods built from these two networks are called actor-critic methods.

Take a look at this figure. The loop runs backward from the game: the reward and the next screen travel back to the critic, and the critic's judgement runs up to the actor. The critic sits between the game and the actor, so each move is judged the moment it is made, not when the game ends. That is the whole trick of this page: a second network that scores moves early.
Section three, One step's surprise
One step's surprise scores the move

Picture the paddle sliding up and the ball heading away, the point still far off. The surprise is the gap between what the critic expected from this screen and what one step actually brought: the reward after the move plus the critic's guess for the next screen, minus the guess here.
How. A positive surprise means the move did better than expected, so the actor makes it more likely; a negative surprise means it did worse, so the actor makes it less likely.
When it works, each move is scored the moment it is made, so good moves are pushed up at once instead of waiting for the game to end.

The target is the reward after the move plus the critic's guess of the next screen, counted a little less by gamma. Putting your own guess for the next state inside the target is called bootstrapping; Q-learning's target does the same.
The TD, temporal difference, error delta is how much one step surprised the agent: the target minus the current guess.
Equation 1. A move can be scored right after it is made, before the point ends.
Take a look at this equation. It scores a move right after it is made.

The surprise line. Delta sub t is the surprise of the move at step t. R sub t plus one is the reward after the move. Plus 1 for a won point, minus 1 for a lost one, 0 otherwise. Gamma is the discount, so the next guess counts a little less. V of s sub t plus one is the critic's guess for the next screen. Minus V of s sub t takes away the guess for this screen. Fee is the weights, the numbers training adjusts. Intuitively, a move is worth its surprise: what one step brought over what the critic expected.
termList: V of s sub t plus one

units.spoken: Intuition. REINFORCE waited for the whole game to judge a move. Here one move is scored the moment it is made, from the surprise it caused.
Example. Take a step where the paddle slides up: no point is won or lost, so the reward is zero, but the guess for the next screen climbs past the guess before the move, so the surprise is positive.
Delta sub t can serve as the move's advantage estimate, A hat sub t: one step's sample of how good the move was, minus the guess of this screen.

A push is the change one update makes to the policy, raising some moves' chances and lowering others. It is biased when, averaged over many games, it points away from the direction that raises J, the average net points per game, fastest. The critic's guess stands in for all the points still to come, so when it is wrong the push trusts a guess that is off the same way every time.

sections.section: 4 Two losses, one for each network, and a bonus to stay undecided

units.spoken: Section four, Two losses, one for each network, and a bonus to stay undecided
One surprise teaches both networks

Picture one Pong step with a positive surprise: the move did better than the critic expected. That one surprise is the actor's credit for the move and also the size of the critic's mistake, so the same number teaches both networks at once.
How. The actor loss pushes the move up by its surprise, and the critic loss pulls the critic's guess toward its target, the old guess corrected by the surprise, so one update trains both networks.
When it works, each step moves both networks at once: the actor's moves get better and the critic's guesses get closer to what actually happens.
Equation 2. The same surprise teaches both networks.
Take a look at this equation. The same surprise teaches both networks.

The actor loss line. L sub actor of thay-ta is the actor loss. Thay-ta is the policy weights, the numbers training adjusts. The sum over t adds over every step in the stretch. Pi sub thay-ta of a sub t given s sub t is the move's chance. Log turns the product of the stretch's chances into a sum, one term per step. A hat sub t is the advantage estimate, here the surprise delta sub t. The minus sign turns the push into a loss to minimize. A hat sub t is held fixed, so only thay-ta changes through this line. Intuitively, the surprise alone must teach the actor: good surprises push their move up, bad ones push it down.
Intuition. The surprise alone must teach the actor over one stretch of play: good surprises push their move up, bad ones push it down.
Example. Take a move that beats the critic's guess: its advantage is positive, so the actor loss pushes its chance up.

The target line. R hat sub t is the target the critic's guess moves toward. The hat means estimate. A hat sub t is the advantage estimate, the surprise. V of s sub t is the guess for this screen. Fee is the weights of the value network. The plus adds the surprise to the guess, correcting it by how much better or worse the move was than expected. Intuitively, the critic needs a target to aim at: its old guess, corrected by the surprise.
Intuition. The critic needs a target to aim at: its old guess, corrected by the surprise.
Example. Take a screen whose guess is too low: the surprise is positive, so the target sits above the old guess.

The critic loss line. L sub critic of fee is the critic loss. Fee is the critic weights, the numbers training adjusts. The sum over t adds over every step in the stretch. Each term squares the brackets, R hat sub t minus V of s sub t, the gap between where the guess should be and where it is. The square makes the gap always positive, so overshooting and undershooting both count. It punishes big misses more than small ones. The target is held fixed, so the guess moves toward its target, and only fee changes through this line. Intuitively, the critic learns from the same surprise: its mistake is the gap between its guess and its target.
Intuition. The critic learns from the same surprise: its mistake is the gap between its guess and its target.
Example. Take a screen whose guess sits below its target: the critic loss pulls the guess up toward it.
So one surprise teaches both networks, pushing each move by its advantage and pulling each guess toward its target.

Take a look at this figure. One step, one surprise, two arrows: the surprise is green, above zero, so the move did better than expected. One arrow runs to the actor, pushing this move up. The other runs to the critic, pulling its guess up toward what happened. The same number teaches both networks at once, in opposite directions.

Entropy, script H, is how undecided the policy is; the entropy bonus rewards staying undecided, so the paddle keeps trying moves it rarely picks. The whole set of move chances on a screen s is written pi sub thay-ta of dot given s.
Equation 3. One loss adds the actor loss and the critic loss, then subtracts a small bonus for staying undecided.
Take a look at this equation. One loss adds the actor loss and the critic loss, then subtracts a small bonus for staying undecided.

The total loss line. L is the total loss. L sub actor pushes the moves and L sub critic fits the critic. C sub V, 0.5 here, sets how much the critic's fit counts. Script H is how undecided the policy is on screen s sub t. The dot stands for all three chances. Script H is high when the moves are about equally likely and zero when one move is certain. The minus in front of c sub H, 0.01 here, means lowering the loss raises the entropy. It pays the paddle to keep trying rare moves. Intuitively, one step must train both networks and still keep the paddle trying new moves.
Intuition. One step must train both networks and still keep the paddle trying new moves.
Example. Take a stretch where stay has won lately, so it gets most of the chance: the entropy there is near zero, so the bonus keeps a sliver on up and down for the paddle to try.
So the whole equation says this: push the moves, fit the critic, and pay a little to stay undecided.

sections.section: 5 Trusting a few real steps first

units.spoken: Section five, Trusting a few real steps first
Count real rewards before trusting the guess

Picture the paddle returning the ball, the point won a few moves later. A lookahead counts a few real rewards first and only then trusts the critic's guess at the far end, so the score leans less on one guess.
How. The lookahead n names how many real rewards are counted: one step trusts the critic at once, the whole return counts real rewards to the end, and n steps sit in between.
When it works, a longer lookahead has less bias from the critic, so the push aims closer to the best direction, though it adds up more random rewards and grows noisier.

Take a look at this figure. Ten steps in a row, two brackets: the short bracket covers one step, the long bracket covers eight. The short one leans on the critic's guess at once. The long one counts eight real rewards first and only then trusts the guess. The longer the bracket, the less the score leans on one guess.
Equation 4. One step leans on the critic; the whole return leans on nothing but real rewards.
Take a look at this equation. One step leans on the critic; the whole return leans on nothing but real rewards.

The n-step line. A hat sub t super n is the n-step advantage estimate. N on top names how many steps it counts, t below names the step it scores. The sum over k runs over the next n steps. Each term is gamma to the k times r sub t plus k plus one. That is the reward k steps ahead. Gamma to the k makes a later reward count less. V of s sub t plus n is the critic's guess n steps ahead. Gamma to the n counts it less. The final minus takes away V of s sub t. At n equal to 1 this is the surprise delta sub t; stretched to the end of the game it is the return minus the guess. Intuitively, one step trusts the critic at once; the whole return trusts nothing but real rewards. Count a few first.
termList: A hat sub t super n
r sub t plus k plus one
V of s sub t plus n

units.spoken: Intuition. One step trusts the critic at once; the whole return trusts nothing but real rewards. Count a few first.

Example. Take a rally where the paddle returns the ball and the point is won soon after: one step trusts the critic's guess at once, while a longer one counts the point first, so its score leans less on that one guess.
So the whole card says this: count a few real rewards first, and the score leans less on one guess.

sections.section: 6 Blending every lookahead with one knob

units.spoken: Section six, Blending every lookahead with one knob
Near lookaheads count most in the blend

Picture every lookahead at once, from one step to the whole game, each scoring the same move a little differently. GAE, generalized advantage estimation, blends them all into one advantage estimate, weighting the near lookaheads most.

How. Lambda sets how slowly the long lookaheads fade: near zero only the shortest counts, near one they all count, the longest nearly as much as the shortest, and each step further out multiplies the weight by gamma times lambda once more.
When it works, no single lookahead has to be right: the blend stays steadier than the one-step surprise and less biased than trusting the critic alone.
Add the surprises of a few steps. Each screen's guess in between is added once and taken away once at the same weight, so it cancels, leaving the real rewards and the guess at the far end.

Take a look at this figure. Three surprises in a row, and the middle guesses cancel: each screen's guess is added once and taken away once at the same weight. Below them, the longer lookaheads fade: fast when lambda is low, slowly when it is high. The blend keeps the real rewards and the guess at the far end, and the near lookaheads count most.
Figure 5 shows three surprises in a row, and below them the longer lookaheads fading fast when lambda is low and slowly when it is high.
Equation 5. Blending every lookahead into one estimate, weighting the near ones most.
Take a look at this equation. Blending every lookahead into one estimate, weighting the near ones most.

The blend line. A hat sub t is the advantage estimate; the hat means estimate. The sum over l adds each later surprise. Delta sub t plus l is the surprise l steps ahead. Gamma lambda to the l is gamma lambda multiplied by itself l times, so each counts less than the one before. Lambda sets how slowly the long lookaheads fade: nearer 0 they fade fast, nearer 1 they fade slowly. The infinity means to the end of the game. With lambda equal to 0 only delta sub t is left; with lambda equal to 1 it is the return minus the guess. Intuitively, no single lookahead is right: blend them all, weighting the near ones most.
Intuition. No single lookahead is right: blend them all, weighting the near ones most.

Example. Take a rally where the paddle's early moves set up a later point: each early surprise is small, while the surprise near the point is large, so the early moves still get some credit for the point.
The spread is how much the push changes from one stretch of play to the next.
Section seven, Many games at once
Many workers, one shared network
Picture four Pong games running side by side, each played by a worker running the current network, so one update sees varied screens instead of one long run of nearly identical ones.

How. In A3C, asynchronous advantage actor-critic, each worker updates the shared network as soon as it is ready; in A2C, advantage actor-critic, all workers wait and update together, joining their steps into one batch, the group of steps an update learns from.
When it works, updates see varied screens, so they no longer all pull the same way, and learning steadies.

One game at a time gives long runs of very similar screens, so a few updates in a row all pull the same way. Policy gradients are on-policy: they learn about the same policy that is playing, counting each move as often as the current policy plays it. Old play holds too many moves the old policy liked, so averaging over it counts those moves too often, and the replay memory of DQN cannot be used here, because it stores old play.

Take a look at this figure. Four games run side by side, all feeding the same network. On the A3C side each worker sends its update the moment it is ready, so the updates land one by one. On the A2C side the workers hold back until all four are ready, then their steps join into a single update. Four games at once give varied screens, so the updates stop pulling the same way.
Each update runs after five steps, and sixteen workers play those steps side by side. The picture shows four workers as a stand-in for sixteen.
In A3C each worker plays a few steps, works out its own update and applies it, without waiting for the others.

A2C waits for every worker and joins their steps into one batch, then makes one update, so every worker plays the next steps with the same new weights. It was made popular by OpenAI Baselines, a set of reference implementations, and it is the one the code in Section 9 builds.
Section eight, Step through one update

Try stepping through the stages with the Prev and Next buttons. Watch the guess curve, then the short and longer lookaheads, the blend, one push arrow per move, and the targets the critic's curve moves toward.
You have now seen each piece on its own card, so this walkthrough follows one Pong update through them, from the circled move to the two losses.
Take a look at this walkthrough. It follows one Pong update through the pieces you have seen.

The one-step stage. The walkthrough draws the critic's guess as the orange curve: it dips after the third move and climbs as the point gets close. The bracket for the one-step lookahead covers one step from the circled move: the reward after it plus the guess of the next screen, minus the guess here. The bracket is green, so the one-step lookahead beat the guess.
Intuition. The one-step lookahead: one step's surprise, from the reward and the critic's two guesses.
Example. Take the circled move: its one-step lookahead is green, so it beat the critic's guess.

The longer lookahead stage. The bracket for the longer lookahead reaches four steps from the circled move, ending at the critic's guess four steps ahead, and it is green, so the longer lookahead beat the guess. Four real rewards count before the critic is trusted, so it leans less on one guess.
Intuition. The longer lookahead: it counts four real rewards before it trusts the critic.
Example. Take the four-step lookahead: it reaches four steps out, so it leans less on one guess.

The blend stage. The walkthrough draws four brackets from the circled move, of lengths one, two, four and six steps, each fainter than the last: the longer lookaheads count less. With lambda equal to 0 only the shortest bracket would count; with lambda equal to 1 they would all count whole.
Intuition. The blended lookaheads: GAE blends every lookahead length, fading the longer ones.
Example. Take the longest bracket, six steps: it is the faintest, so the far surprises count least.

The push stage. The walkthrough draws one push arrow per move: green and up where its blended estimate is positive, red and down where it is negative. Six arrows point up and one points down: the one pointing down is the third move, whose blended estimate is negative.
Intuition. The push arrows: the actor pushes each move by its blended estimate.
Example. Take the third move: its arrow points down, so the actor makes it less likely.

The target stage. The walkthrough draws the targets as green dots, each one its screen's guess plus its blended estimate, and the new solid curve moved toward them, closer to the dots than the old dashed curve. A dot above the old curve goes with a green push, and a dot below the old curve goes with a red push.
Intuition. The new curve and its targets: the critic's curve moves toward the green dots.
Example. Take the third dot: it sits below the old curve, so its push is red and down.

Summary. Take the step the walkthrough shows: the circled move goes up as the ball comes in high, and a point is won near the end of the stretch. The critic's guess dips after the third move and climbs as the point gets close, so the surprises along the stretch are mixed, the blend gives the circled move a positive advantage, the actor pushes it up, and the critic's curve moves toward the dots, its targets.

Figure 7 shows one short stretch and one update: the game, the critic's guess, the lookaheads, the pushes and the targets. The stages walk through the update in order: the guess curve, the short lookahead and then the longer one, the blend, where longer lookaheads count less, one push arrow per move, and the targets the critic's curve moves toward. The first two stages highlight no line, and each later stage highlights one line of the loss below, from the surprise to the two losses.

Take a look at this figure. The shortest lookahead: one real reward, then the critic's guess for the next screen. The green bracket starts at the circled move and ends one step ahead. Green means it beat the guess, so the surprise is positive. This is the one-step surprise, drawn as a bracket.

Figure 8 shows the shortest lookahead: one real reward, then the critic's guess for the next screen. The green bracket starts at the circled move and ends one step ahead, at the diamond on the critic's guess. Green means the lookahead beat the guess, so the surprise is positive.

Take a look at this figure. The longer lookahead: four real rewards before the critic's guess is trusted. The green bracket starts at the circled move and ends four steps ahead. Green means this longer lookahead also beat the guess, so it leans less on one guess. Compare it with the short one: the same move, the same guess at the far end, but four real rewards counted first.

Figure 9 shows the longer lookahead: four real rewards before the critic's guess is trusted. The green bracket starts at the circled move and ends four steps ahead, at the diamond on the critic's guess. Green means this longer lookahead also beat the guess, so it leans less on one guess.
Section nine, Actor-Critic in PyTorch

A toy A2C for Pong, to read rather than run; Pong offers six actions, and we keep the three that move the paddle. The code uses gymnasium, the library that runs the games, and ale_py, the Atari game set it loads. Some of its settings follow the Stable-Baselines3 A2C defaults; Stable-Baselines3 is a library of ready-made reinforcement learning algorithms.

This code builds a toy A2C for Pong: one shared network with an actor head and a critic head, and a loop that plays five steps, works out the GAE blend and the two losses, and takes one optimizer step.
1. Copies of Pong in one batch, each played by the same network; a finished game restarts within the same step, so every step is a real move.
2. One shared body with two outputs: the actor's raw outputs, called logits, for the three moves, and the critic's guess V of s, with weights fee.
3. GAE, added up backward: each step's surprise, then the blend; the mask is one minus dones, which drops the next guess when the game ended.

4. The stretch of play: the network and its RMSProp, root mean square propagation, optimizer are built first, then each game plays a few steps and the moves, rewards and guesses are collected for the two losses.

5. The two losses: returns is R hat sub t, and detach() holds A hat sub t and R hat sub t fixed. The equations add over steps; the code takes the average over steps instead, which is the same total divided by the number of steps.
6. The whole loss, then one step with the optimizer built in note 4; clip_grad_norm_ caps the size of the gradient.

sections.section: 10 How λ trades bias for spread

units.spoken: Section ten, How lambda trades bias for spread

At each numbered spot the paddle chooses between two moves: the helpful move, which sends it back well, and the other, which sends it back badly. The critic has the two moves backwards: after the helpful move it guesses too low, after the other too high. The true value is what the critic would guess knowing the points still to come exactly. The true push is the push with no bias from the critic.

Try moving lambda with the slider, and resample to draw a fresh stretch of play. At lambda equal to 0 the bold arrows point against the helpful move, but the faint arrows sit in a tight band. At lambda equal to 1 the bold tips land on the dark ticks, but the faint arrows fan nearly the whole lane wide. Watch the bold arrows move toward the true push as the faint arrows spread.

Figure 10 shows how lambda trades bias for spread: faint arrows are one stretch's push, the bold arrow their average, the dark tick the true push. At lambda equal to 0 the bold arrows point against the helpful move and the faint arrows sit in a tight band, all left of centre; at lambda equal to 1 the bold tips land on the dark ticks, but the faint arrows fan nearly the whole lane wide.

sections.section: 11 The settings and what each one does

units.spoken: Section eleven, The settings and what each one does
The learning rate eta, the lr in the code, sets how big a step each update takes.
One update runs the network forward over one batch of steps, then one backward pass; the memory it holds grows with that batch.

This table is the settings for actor-critic on Atari. Workers is 16: more workers mean more varied screens and faster play, fewer mean runs of similar screens. Steps per update is 5: more steps mean longer lookaheads, less bias and more noise, fewer mean shorter lookaheads that lean on the critic. The discount gamma is 0.99: higher means far-off points count more, less bias and more noise, lower means only near points count, more bias. The entropy weight c sub H is 0.01: higher stays undecided longer and settles slower, lower commits sooner and may lock on. The learning rate eta is 7 times 10 to the minus 4: higher is faster until overshoot, lower is steadier and slower. Lambda is 0.9 to 0.99: higher means less bias and more spread, lower means less spread and more bias. The critic-loss weight c sub V is 0.5: higher means the critic learns faster but can crowd out the actor, lower means the critic lags and its bias lasts longer. The gradient cap is 0.5: higher means bigger, riskier steps, lower means safer, slower steps. The pattern is the field's defaults, each row naming its source.
Each row names its source, so the values are the ones the field uses, not guesses.
Section twelve, When Actor-Critic fits
A discrete move is one choice from a short list, up, stay or down; a continuous move is a real number.

This table lines up when each method fits. Actor-critic fits long games with late rewards and cheap play: each move is judged a few steps on, each stretch is used once, and it takes discrete and continuous, real-number, moves. Deep Q-Networks fits costly play, because replay reuses each stretch many times. REINFORCE fits short games, where waiting until the end costs little: it has no critic to train, so its return is unbiased but noisy. The pattern is the price of play against the price of waiting: cheap play and late rewards favor the critic, costly play favors replay, short games favor waiting.
Picture the paddle sliding to any height on the court instead of only up, stay or down.
Section thirteen, What breaks Actor-Critic

This table lists what breaks Actor-Critic, each symptom with its cause and its fix. The paddle drifts toward worse moves when a wrong critic biases the push: raise lambda or c sub V. Training runs end far apart when lambda is too high: lower lambda. Learning swings back and forth with one worker only, because updates see similar screens: add workers. The paddle stops being undecided too early when c sub H is too small: raise c sub H. Learning blows up when the learning rate is too high: lower eta and cap the step. Updates fight each other in A3C when workers apply updates worked out on old weights: switch to A2C. The pattern is that every break traces back to the critic, the workers, or the step size, and each fix names which one.

sections.section: 14 Using each stretch of play once

units.spoken: Section fourteen, Using each stretch of play once
Each stretch of play feeds a single update and is then thrown away, so could the same batch be reused without the pushes going wrong? Proximal Policy Optimization, PPO, sets out to answer that.
